name: Cetirizine topical

lead: Topical cetirizine is a lotion form of a common allergy drug, explored for androgenetic alopecia. The goal is thicker hair and less thinning by protecting follicles from miniaturisation.

The idea is that prostaglandin D2 contributes to follicle shrinkage, and cetirizine blocks related inflammation signalling. A phase 2/3 trial, NCT04481412, in 66 women with androgenetic alopecia started in 2020 and was completed; no results were available for this entry.

paras: It is investigational for hair, applied as a lotion to the scalp in the trial setting. It is used off-label by some people outside trials.
Oral cetirizine can cause drowsiness. Scalp-specific safety data were not reviewed.

angle.text: Topical cetirizine is explored as a hair-loss lotion on the theory that blocking prostaglandin D2 signalling protects follicles from shrinking, keeping hair thicker. It is an allergy drug used off-label for this. It has been tested in a small trial in women, and results are not confirmed.

lead: Topical cetirizine is a lotion, typically around 1%, made from the second-generation antihistamine cetirizine and investigated as a scalp treatment for androgenetic alopecia (pattern hair loss). The idea is that prostaglandin D2 (PGD2) in the scalp contributes to hair-follicle miniaturisation, and that an antihistamine applied to the scalp could reduce that signal and help preserve or thicken hair, giving a fuller look.[1][2]

Small clinical studies have tested it in both men and women. A randomised trial of 66 women with female pattern hair loss compared cetirizine plus minoxidil against placebo plus minoxidil for 24 weeks and reported greater improvements in terminal and vellus hair density, shaft thickness and self-assessment in the cetirizine group.[3][2] A study of 60 men reported more dermoscopic regrowth and higher satisfaction than placebo after six months.[2]

A 2022 systematic review of three trials, all at moderate-to-high risk of bias, judged cetirizine likely better than placebo, and described it as appearing less effective than minoxidil for density but about equal for hair diameter, calling for larger randomised trials.[2] Topical cetirizine is not an approved hair-loss product; cetirizine itself is a widely used oral allergy drug, first patented by UCB in 1983.[1]
infobox: Oral cetirizine is OTC in many countries; topical hair use is off-label

paras: Cetirizine selectively blocks peripheral histamine H1 receptors and has described anti-inflammatory effects involving NF-kB suppression.[1] The hair-loss rationale, as stated by investigators, is that cetirizine lowers prostaglandin D2, which has been reported to inhibit hair growth.[2]

Orally, cetirizine treats allergic rhinitis and hives; trials have examined it for conditions such as seasonal rhinitis and rash prevention.[4][5] Topical 1% cetirizine is an investigational hair-loss approach tested in androgenetic alopecia, including in combination with minoxidil and with microneedling.[2][6]

Oral use commonly causes drowsiness, dry mouth and headache; after prolonged daily use, stopping can cause severe itching, per an FDA Drug Safety Communication in May 2025.[1][7] In the female trial, side effects did not differ significantly between the cetirizine and placebo groups,[2] and a preliminary study reported no notable side effects from topical use.[6]

The published topical studies are small. A 2021 case-controlled study in 60 men aged 22 to 55 compared daily 1% cetirizine with placebo for six months and reported significantly greater dermoscopic regrowth and higher satisfaction; the authors called for more randomised trials.[2] A randomised, double-blind trial published in 2023 in 66 women aged 20 to 50 reported that adding cetirizine to minoxidil improved density and thickness over minoxidil alone.[2] The registered phase 2/3 trial NCT04481412 in 66 women was completed.[3]

A 2022 systematic review of three trials rated all as moderate-to-high risk of bias and suggested cetirizine may suit people who respond poorly to minoxidil.[2] Later studies include a 2025 trial of cetirizine with microneedling in men and a 2025 preliminary study, reported in a PubMed listing.[6]
UCB patented cetirizine in 1983.[1] Topical use for hair loss appeared in the literature by 2017, with a preliminary clinical study published in 2018.[6]

timeline.event: A letter on topical 1% cetirizine for androgenetic alopecia appears in Dermatologic Therapy.[2]
Female androgenetic alopecia trial of topical cetirizine begins.[3]
A systematic review of three topical cetirizine trials is published.[2]
